title: State-simplex trajectory (3D, coloured by log time): does the orbit stay physical?
summary: Mole or mass fractions that must add to one live on a triangle. This plot draws a three-species trajectory in the corner-to-corner geometry of the simplex, coloured by logarithmic time, with the exact and the learned orbit overlaid.

media.alt: Three-dimensional plot of a triangle (the simplex) with corners S1, S2, S3: coloured dots (log time from purple to yellow) run from S1 along an edge towards S2, curve at the S2 corner and run along an edge to S3; an amber dashed learned curve follows closely.
media.caption: Reference render of class F6.3 (design-system gallery). The data are synthetic and exist only to demonstrate the form.

source.note: Plot class from the design system's plot taxonomy; synthetic demonstration data.

read_the_figure.question: Does the orbit stay physical?
read_the_figure.axes: Three axes y1, y2, y3, each 0 to 1. The triangle with vertices S1 = (1,0,0), S2 = (0,1,0), S3 = (0,0,1) is the physical region y1 + y2 + y3 = 1, y_i at least 0. Colour: log10 of time in seconds (-3 to 2).
look_at: Does the orbit stay on the triangle (inside the simplex edges), or does it leave?
Where is the orbit at early, middle and late time? Follow the colour from purple to yellow.
Where do the exact (dots) and learned (dashed) orbits separate, and by how much?
Are the vertices labelled and the constraint stated?
as_drawn: The exact orbit starts at S1 (purple), runs along the S1 to S2 edge, turns near S2 (teal-green, around log10 t = 0 to 0.2) and runs along the S2 to S3 edge to S3 (yellow, log10 t = 2).
The amber dashed learned orbit overlays the exact one on the first edge, cuts slightly inside the corner near S2 and runs a little inside the second edge.
The triangle's edges are drawn white and its face is lightly shaded; the footnote states that the orbit stays on y1 + y2 + y3 = 1 with y_i at least 0.
The picture is a 3D perspective view; a flat ternary diagram would show the same facts without foreshortening.
read_the_figure.proves: If the learned orbit stays inside the simplex and follows the exact one, the model respects the physical constraints and tracks the right sequence of species. A visual overlay does not quantify the error: it cannot show differences smaller than the marker size.
if_wrong: Orbit leaves the triangle (a negative fraction or a sum other than one): the model does not conserve mass or positivity.
Learned curve cuts the corner: the peak of the intermediate species is underestimated.
Colour not log time: the long late period would be crushed into one colour.
must_check: simplex edges: they show the physical region, so a point outside is visibly wrong.
exact versus learned overlay: the claim is about the model, so the reference must be on the same plot.

terms.meaning: The set of non-negative fractions that sum to one; for three species a triangle.
A corner of the simplex, where one species is pure and the others are zero.
The share of the total mass (or moles) in one species.
The path traced by the state as time advances.
A fitted model (for example a neural network) whose trajectory is compared with the exact one.
Colour encodes log10 t, so each colour step is a constant factor in time.

remember: Sum of fractions = 1 and each fraction at least 0: inside the triangle.
Ternary coordinates: u = y2 + y3/2, v = (sqrt(3)/2) y3 draw the triangle flat.
A to B to C kinetics: B peaks at t* = ln(k1/k2) / (k1 - k2).
A model respects the physics if its orbit never leaves the simplex.
Colour by log time to see all the scales.

understand.title: Marks and encodings
understand.text: Position in the 3D box encodes the three fractions. Dots are the exact solution, coloured by log time from purple (early) to yellow (late); the amber dashed line is the learned model. White lines are the triangle's edges and the labels S1, S2, S3 mark the pure-species corners. The colour bar gives the log time scale.

understand.title: Why this form answers the question
understand.text: Plain language: if three amounts must add to one, every possible state is a point on a triangle. A reaction moves the point from one corner to another. Drawing the triangle makes a physical constraint visible: a model that breaks mass balance or gives a negative amount leaves the triangle, which you can see without any calculation. Overlaying the learned orbit on the exact one answers whether it follows the right route.

understand.title: How it misleads
understand.text: Perspective foreshortens: two points that look close can be far apart in the third direction. The dots are drawn with a fixed size, so an error smaller than the marker is invisible; and the colour compresses the very early and very late stages. A close overlay on the simplex does not mean the timing is right, because the plot shows the route and not how fast it is travelled except through colour.

understand.title: Alternatives
understand.text: A flat ternary diagram removes the perspective. Plotting each fraction against log time and the error against time shows timing and accuracy directly. For quantitative claims, plot the distance between exact and learned against time.

understand.title: A variant to create
understand.text: Redraw it as a flat ternary diagram with gridlines every 0.1, add small arrows showing the direction of travel at log10 t = -2, 0, 2, and add a separate panel with the distance between the two orbits against time.

steps.title: The constraint and the flat picture
steps.note: The map to the plane places S1 at (0,0), S2 at (1,0) and S3 at (1/2, sqrt(3)/2): an equilateral triangle.

steps.title: A to B to C kinetics
steps.note: Verified numerically: the three sum to 1 to machine precision and are non-negative. With k1 = 2 and k2 = 0.15 this is the exact orbit in the render.

steps.title: When the middle species peaks
steps.note: For k1 = 2, k2 = 0.15 this is t* = 1.40 s and y2 = 0.81: the orbit passes close to the S2 corner, at log10 t = 0.15.

worked.title: Reading the orbit from the reference render
worked.problem: (1) Between which corners does the orbit travel, and in which order? (2) At about what time does it pass nearest S2, and how close does it get? (3) What conditions must a point satisfy to be on the simplex, and does the learned curve satisfy them?

solution.text: (1) From S1 along the first edge to near S2, then along the second edge to S3; the colour runs from purple to yellow.
(2) The turn is in the teal-green dots, around log10 t = 0 to 0.2. Compute the model's peak.
So the orbit passes within about 0.19 of the S2 corner in the y2 coordinate.
(3) The conditions are that each fraction is at least zero and that the three sum to one.
The learned curve stays inside the triangle in the render, cutting the corner at S2, which means it underestimates the peak of the intermediate species by a small amount.

worked.answer: S1 to S2 to S3; nearest S2 at about 1.4 s with y2 of 0.81; the learned curve respects the simplex but cuts the S2 corner slightly.

analyze.q: The exact orbit hugs the edges of the triangle. What does that say about the reaction?
analyze.hint: On an edge one fraction is zero.

analyze.q: The learned curve cuts inside the corner at S2. What physical quantity is being underestimated and why might a network do that?
analyze.hint: Peak of the intermediate species; smooth approximation.

analyze.q: Why would a perspective 3D view be a poor choice for a quantitative claim?

evaluate.q: The learned curve is inside the simplex and looks close to the exact one. Is the model validated?
evaluate.hint: Timing, error versus time, other initial conditions.

create: Draw the same orbit on a flat ternary diagram with a distance-to-exact curve beside it.
Add a second initial condition (start near S2) and show the two orbits in different colours.

checks.q: Why is the physical region a triangle?
checks.answer: Three non-negative fractions that sum to one: two independent numbers, with the sum constraint fixing a flat triangle whose corners are the pure species.

checks.q: k1 = 1 and k2 = 0.5. When does the middle species peak and how high is it?
checks.hint: t* and the formula for y2 at t*.

checks.q: A learned orbit leaves the triangle slightly near S2. List two likely causes.
checks.hint: What would a model need to enforce?
checks.answer: It does not enforce positivity or the sum constraint (for example an unconstrained output layer), or it extrapolates a sharp peak badly; remedies are a softmax output or a constrained parametrisation.
